good_morning.note: Xhosa greetings are not inherently time-specific: Molo alone covers any time of day, and Omniglot's phrasebook lists plain Molo for 'good day/afternoon/evening' with no separate morning form. Ekuseni ('in the morning') tacked on is a plain, understandable build-up rather than a fixed idiom, so treat this as a lower-confidence construction, not a set phrase.

good_evening.note: Same construction pattern as Molo ekuseni, adding ngokuhlwa ('in the evening'); Omniglot's own 'Good evening' entry is just plain Molo, so this compound is understandable but not a fixed idiom, and should be read as a lower-confidence build rather than an attested set phrase.

goodbye.note: Said by the one leaving, literally 'stay well'; the one staying replies Hamba kakuhle (HAHM-bah kah-KOO-hleh), 'go well'.

how_are_you.note: To more than one person: Ninjani? (nee-n-JAH-nee).

thank_you.note: The everyday word; the fuller Ndiyabulela (ndee-yah-boo-LEH-lah) is more formal.

youre_welcome.note: Literally 'you are welcomed'; the standard reply to Enkosi.

no_problem.note: Literally 'there is no problem'; casual, brushing off a favor or small mishap. The ngx is a nasalized click, see the note on Uxolo.

please.note: Literally 'help'; the everyday way to soften a request. Ndicela (ndee-CHEH-lah), 'I ask/request', is a milder alternative tacked onto the front of a sentence.

excuse_me.note: Xhosa has three click letters: c (dental, like a disapproving 'tsk'), q (a sharp pop made at the roof of the mouth), and x (a sideways click made against the side teeth, like the sound used to call a horse). Respellings here use kh, hl, ngx, etc. only to hint at the mouth shape; a native speaker's click will sound sharper and is made with the tongue, not the throat.

sorry.note: More formal apology than Uxolo; fine for real mistakes, not just minor bumps.

of_course.note: Literally 'yes indeed'; impela alone also stands as a firm 'definitely'. This is a plain, transparent build from two independently attested words (Ewe='yes' on Omniglot; impela='indeed' cross-checked via GT) rather than a documented single-word idiom for 'of course' — Xhosa phrase lists don't give one, so treat as lower confidence than the other entries.

amazing.note: Literally 'it is amazing/astonishing'; a warm way to say something blew you away.

delicious.note: Also just means 'nice/pleasant/fun'; the go-to compliment for a cook.

cheers.note: Literally 'health!'; the toast said when raising a glass, same root as Zulu's word for health.
